absent: Behavior of the single-group create and update worker and full file removal beyond the visible tail, including visibility and update-mode merge rules.
Kernfs lookup, creation, rename, removal, reference counting and namespace semantics and their locking.
Kobject ownership, naming, lifetime and duplicate-warning rules.
Network namespace and user namespace capture, permission and superblock flag handling beyond the checks shown.
Alarm and high-resolution timer start, forward, cancel and callback concurrency guarantees.
Time-namespace translation, timespec conversion and monotonic to realtime offset semantics.
Anonymous inode, descriptor allocation, poll table, wait queue and iterator copy semantics.
Workqueue scheduling guarantees for deferred resume handling.
Exact numeric values of magic, flags, clocks, error codes and control commands.
Configuration conditions selecting null versus active descriptor info and control variants.

findings.text: Exposes kernel interfaces to create, refresh and remove attribute groups on an object, singly and as null-terminated lists, plus merge and unmerge of extra attributes into an existing named directory and addition and removal of links inside a named group. Creation and refresh share a common worker distinguished by an update mode; removal tolerates absent groups.

Exposes kernel interfaces to create links either under a given object or under the filesystem root when no object is supplied, with warning and quiet variants for name collisions, plus namespace-aware deletion, plain removal by name, conditional rename across namespaces, and a compatibility helper that links an entry found inside another object.

Registers a filesystem type for the synthetic object hierarchy with context setup and teardown operations. Setup enforces mount permission for namespace-aware mounts, anchors the shared root and filesystem identity, captures the current network namespace and adopts its user namespace. Teardown releases namespace references after delegating superblock destruction.

Provides timer file creation and time programming and query through system calls and a file operations table binding release, poll, read, seek, descriptor info and control operations. Creation validates requested clock and flags and enforces privilege for wake-capable alarm clocks; programming validates flags and timer specification and reports prior settings; query reports current remaining time and interval.
System-wide notification entry points allow resume processing to be deferred to work context and clock-change processing to invalidate registered timers and wake waiters.

Timer file private state combines a dual timer holder usable either as high-resolution timer or alarm, a periodic interval, a clock offset marker, a wait queue for poll and read wakeups, a tick counter, a clock identifier, expiry and flag fields for descriptor info, deferred reclamation linkage, cancel-list linkage with its own guard and a membership flag.

Filesystem global state consists of a shared root pointer and its node pointer, a per-mount context holding a namespace tag, a root reference and a magic identity, an operations table binding free and tree acquisition, and a filesystem type descriptor binding name, context setup, superblock teardown and user-namespace mount properties.

A dedicated spin lock guards sampling of a target object backing node and its namespace because targets may detach concurrently. Holders take a reference while holding the lock and release after, and never retain the sampled pointer without that reference.

A wait-queue lock guards tick count, expiry marker and offset marker and is held across trigger, poll inspection, read consumption and reprogramming; a per-file cancel guard plus a global cancel guard protect membership in a global cancel list; clock-change notification uses read-side traversal with per-file queue locking.

Named groups exist as child directories with attribute and link members; unnamed groups attach directly to the parent node. Transitions add a directory then members, or members into an existing directory, and removal detaches members then the directory when named. List creation is all-or-nothing; merge is all-or-nothing within one call; unmerge and removal of absent members converge to absent.

A timer file moves among disarmed, armed, expired-signalled and cancelled-on-clock-change conditions. Arming clears prior counts and expiry; expiry sets signalled state and increments ticks; consumption clears signalled state and counts and may rearm periodic timers; clock-change notification forces the cancelled condition requiring user re-evaluation.

Group list operations treat a null list as success with no effect and otherwise provide rollback: failure while creating a list removes earlier members of that list, and failure while merging removes the subset already added by that call. Removal of a missing named group is a no-op with diagnostic logging rather than an error.

Link creation rejects missing names or parents, reports missing when the target is already detached, reports collision on duplicate names with optional duplicate warning, and defaults a null parent object to the filesystem root. Rename requires the existing entry to be a link bound to the expected target and honours old and new namespaces; deletion honours the target namespace when enabled.

Periodic rearming is deferred out of timer callbacks; immediate expiry at start time is treated as already triggered; remaining time is clamped at zero; absolute expiries pass through time-namespace translation; cancel-on-set membership applies only to realtime clocks with absolute and cancel flags; alarm versus high-resolution handling is selected by clock identity.

File operations verify the descriptor really belongs to this facility before use; alarm clocks require wake-alarm privilege at creation and at programming; creation and programming reject unknown flag bits and unsupported clocks or invalid specifications; descriptor info and control entry points may be compiled out to null.

Targets and group directories may vanish concurrently, so callers must tolerate missing results and must not assume a previously resolved node remains valid without a held reference. Duplicate link or attribute names collide; compatibility linking defaults a missing link name to the entry name which increases collision risk.

Reprogramming must cope with a callback in flight by dropping locks and waiting for completion before proceeding. Very short periods must not be rearmed in interrupt context. Reads need an eight-byte minimum, may block or fail fast depending on nonblock state, and a clock change converts a pending read into a cancellation report with cleared counts.

Filesystem identity facts include the registered type name and magic value, user-namespace mount capability flags, a global-mount marking on new contexts, and an internal header guard macro. Group and link operations signal missing entries with a not-found status and invalid requests with an invalid-argument status.

Timer facility identity facts include the supported monotonic, realtime, realtime-alarm, boottime and boottime-alarm clock selectors, creation and programming flag masks, a tick-injection control command, poll readability signalled through input readiness, and descriptor info fields reporting clock identity, tick count, flags, current value and interval.
